[super-qa] high: Orphan .pak.tmp file on serialization or encoder-flush failure
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Orphan .pak.tmp file on serialization or encoder-flush failure**

- **ID:** `archive/correctness-tmp-file-leak`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/archive/pak.rs:38-43`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
In `write_pak_and_hash`, if `serde_json::to_writer` or `encoder.finish()` returns an error, the function early-returns via `?` but the temp file (`path.with_extension("pak.tmp")`) already exists on disk and is never deleted. Repeated failures accumulate stale `.pak.tmp` files in the archive directory. The atomic write guarantee (tmp+rename) only protects against a half-written final file, not against cleanup of the temp file itself on the failure path.

## Suggested approach
Use a guard struct or an explicit cleanup on all error paths:
```rust
struct TmpGuard<'a> { path: &'a Path, committed: bool }
impl Drop for TmpGuard<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) { if !self.committed { let _ = fs::remove_file(self.path); } }
}
// After fs::rename succeeds, call guard.committed = true;
```
Or at minimum add `let _ = fs::remove_file(&tmp_path);` before each error `?` propagation.

## References
CWE-459: Incomplete Cleanup

<!-- super-qa-key: archive/correctness-tmp-file-leak -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] high: Orphan .pak file on commit_archive failure leaves unregistered pak on disk
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Orphan .pak file on commit_archive failure leaves unregistered pak on disk**

- **ID:** `archive/correctness-orphan-pak-on-commit-failure`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/engine/archive.rs:65-79`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
The archive orchestration sequence is: (1) `write_pak_to_disk` (writes and renames `.pak`), then (2) `commit_archive` (SQLite manifest insert + hard-delete in one transaction). If `commit_archive` fails after step 1, the `.pak` file exists on disk but has no manifest row and the facts are still in the live DB. On the next `archive()` call with the same policy, the same candidates are selected again and a second `.pak` is written with a different timestamp filename — the first pak is never registered and accumulates as an orphan. Over time, disk space is silently leaked. There is no recovery or orphan-detection mechanism.

## Suggested approach
Add a pre-commit cleanup step: before writing the new pak, scan the archive directory for `*.pak` files not referenced in the manifest table, log and optionally delete them. Alternatively, register a provisional manifest row (with a `status='pending'` column) before writing the pak file, then upgrade it to `status='committed'` inside the SQLite transaction that also hard-deletes the facts; abandoned rows with `status='pending'` can be cleaned up on engine open.

## References
CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

<!-- super-qa-key: archive/correctness-orphan-pak-on-commit-failure -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] high: Stale in-memory importance_score causes incorrect inheritance in multi-duplicate chains
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Stale in-memory importance_score causes incorrect inheritance in multi-duplicate chains**

- **ID:** `consolidation/correctness-stale-importance-score`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** consolidation · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/consolidation/dedup.rs:93-103`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
After `fact_store.update_importance_score(survivor.id, loser.importance_score)` (line 102), the survivor's `importance_score` field in the in-memory `active_facts` Vec is NOT updated. Subsequent comparisons in the outer `new_facts` loop that involve the same survivor as a candidate use its stale in-memory value. Concrete scenario with three near-duplicates A (score=0.3), B (score=0.8), C (score=0.5), all equal base importance, ids A < B < C: (1) new_fact=A vs candidate=B → expire B, B.score(0.8) > A.score(0.3) → DB update A to 0.8, but A.score in memory stays 0.3. (2) new_fact=A vs candidate=C → expire C, C.score(0.5) > A.score(0.3 stale) → DB update A to 0.5, overwriting the correct 0.8. Final DB importance_score for A is 0.5, but the correct max-of-all is 0.8. The existing test `survivor_inherits_max_importance` only exercises the two-fact case and does not catch this.

## Suggested approach
Maintain a `HashMap<i64, f64>` (indexed by fact id) alongside `expired_ids` to track the running maximum importance_score for each survivor within the loop. Replace the in-memory read `survivor.importance_score` with a lookup in that map before deciding whether to issue the DB update. Alternatively, use a mutable Vec of (id, importance_score) tuples that is updated in place when a survivor gains a higher score. The same stale-read concern applies to `importance` (via `update_importance` at line 99), though in that case the condition is structurally unreachable given that `expire_id` is always the lower-importance fact — verify and document this invariant, or guard symmetrically.

## References

<!-- super-qa-key: consolidation/correctness-stale-importance-score -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] high: Orphaned .pak file on commit_archive failure
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Orphaned .pak file on commit_archive failure**

- **ID:** `engine/correctness-orphan-pak`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** core · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/engine/archive.rs:65-80`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
In archive(), write_pak_to_disk() writes the .pak file to disk (line 65), then commit_archive() is called with ? (line 72). If commit_archive fails (DB error, disk-full, etc.), the .pak file is left permanently on disk with no manifest entry and no cleanup. This is a latent disk-leak: subsequent verify_archives() calls will fail to reconcile the orphan. The restore.rs module handles the same pattern correctly via let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&config.path) in its error paths (restore.rs:127).

## Suggested approach
Capture the pak path before calling commit_archive, then add an on-error cleanup: let pak_path = config.path.clone(); self.commit_archive(...).inspect_err(|_| { let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&pak_path); })?;

## References
CWE-459

<!-- super-qa-key: engine/correctness-orphan-pak -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] high: flush_insights accepts unbounded insights array from untrusted MCP caller
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**flush_insights accepts unbounded insights array from untrusted MCP caller**

- **ID:** `mcp/correctness-flush-insights-no-cap`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** mcp · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `memory-engine-mcp/src/tools/mod.rs:840-843`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
The `handle_flush_insights` handler reads the `insights` array directly from client JSON with no `maxItems` cap — neither in the JSON schema definition (`all_tool_definitions`) nor in the handler logic. An untrusted MCP client can send an arbitrarily large array; the handler iterates every element, allocates `AddFactRequest` objects, embeds each via the HTTP provider, and inserts them all within a single `spawn_blocking` call. This creates a CPU/memory/network DoS vector bounded only by the tokio blocking thread pool timeout and available RAM. The JSON Schema for `memory_flush_insights` has no `maxItems` constraint.

## Suggested approach
Add a server-side cap (e.g., 1000 items) at the start of `handle_flush_insights`: `if insights.len() > MAX_FLUSH_BATCH { return Err(ErrorData::invalid_params("insights exceeds maximum batch size", None)); }`. Also add `"maxItems": 1000` to the JSON schema property for `insights` in `all_tool_definitions`.

<!-- super-qa-key: mcp/correctness-flush-insights-no-cap -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] high: bootstrap_session accepts unbounded jsonl_data string from untrusted MCP caller
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**bootstrap_session accepts unbounded jsonl_data string from untrusted MCP caller**

- **ID:** `mcp/correctness-bootstrap-no-size-cap`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** mcp · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `memory-engine-mcp/src/tools/mod.rs:1225-1239`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`handle_bootstrap_session` reads `jsonl_data` from client JSON (line 1225) with no length limit, then materializes it entirely into a `Cursor<Vec<u8>>` via `jsonl_data.into_bytes()` at line 1239. A multi-MB or multi-GB string allocates an equivalent byte buffer on the blocking thread pool before any processing begins. The JSON schema for `memory_bootstrap_session` has no `maxLength` constraint on `jsonl_data`. There is no streaming: the entire buffer is held in memory for the duration of the bootstrap operation.

## Suggested approach
Add a maximum size check before `into_bytes()`: `if jsonl_data.len() > MAX_JSONL_BYTES { return Err(ErrorData::invalid_params("jsonl_data exceeds maximum size", None)); }`. Also add `"maxLength"` to the JSON schema property. For large-data use cases, consider accepting a filesystem path to the JSONL file rather than an inline string.

manifest.title: [super-qa] high: idx_activities_dedup index column count diverges between fresh install and migration path
manifest.body:
> ✅ **Verified against primary source.** VERIFIED: migrate line687=5cols(+scope_id) vs TABLES_DDL line819=4cols

**idx_activities_dedup index column count diverges between fresh install and migration path**

- **ID:** `store/design-schema-ddl-divergence`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/store/schema.rs:686-687 (migrate_v8_to_v9) vs src/store/schema.rs:818-819 (TABLES_DDL)`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
TABLES_DDL (line 819) defines `idx_activities_dedup ON activities(session_id, tool_name, args_hash, outcome_class)` — 4 columns. migrate_v8_to_v9 (line 687) defines it as `ON activities(session_id, tool_name, args_hash, outcome_class, scope_id)` — 5 columns. A freshly-initialized database gets the narrower index; a migrated database gets the wider one. The indexes have different selectivity and serve different query shapes. Any deduplication query that relies on scope_id being part of the index will miss the optimization on fresh installs, and vice versa. Silent behavioral divergence between new and upgraded deployments.

## Suggested approach
Decide the canonical index definition and apply it in both TABLES_DDL and migrate_v8_to_v9. If scope_id belongs in the index (wider), add it to TABLES_DDL line 819. If not, remove it from the migration. Then add a regression test that initializes via init_schema and a test-migrated DB and asserts both have the same index definition via `PRAGMA index_info(idx_activities_dedup)`.

## References
https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_index_info

<!-- super-qa-key: store/design-schema-ddl-divergence -->

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**`Fact` has two importance fields with near-identical names but different semantics**

- **ID:** `core-root/design-importance-field-ambiguity`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** core · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/types.rs:133-139`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
Current state: `Fact` (types.rs:133) has `pub importance: f64` (the caller-supplied base seed stored at insert time) and `pub importance_score: f64` (the materialized computed score updated by the forgetting pipeline). The distinction is confirmed by store/facts.rs:95 comment `// seed importance_score from base importance` and the existence of `update_importance_score` vs no `update_importance`. Target state: rename to make semantics self-documenting — `importance_seed: f64` or `base_importance: f64` for the caller hint, and retain `importance_score` for the computed materialized value. Refactoring pattern: Rename field for semantic clarity. Motivation: readability and coupling — callers reading the struct see two `f64` fields whose difference is not apparent without reading engine internals; the forgetting pipeline uses `importance_score` for decay comparisons (engine/query.rs:241) but `Fact.importance` is also read by engine tests (engine/tests.rs:400, 470), making it easy to confuse the two when writing new queries or forgetting logic. Estimated scope: types.rs, store/facts.rs, engine/ingest.rs, and all test sites (5-8 files). Prerequisites: decide on the canonical rename before touching call sites. Risk: medium — pure rename, no semantic change, but touches many files.

## Suggested approach
Rename `Fact.importance` to `Fact.base_importance` (and `NewFact.importance` to `NewFact.base_importance`) everywhere in the workspace. Update the SQL column name in a schema migration if the DB column is also named `importance`.

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Implementation submodules exposed as `pub` despite no external callers**

- **ID:** `inspect/design-impl-submodules-overcalibrated-pub`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/inspect/mod.rs:6-11`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
All five implementation submodules (`dump`, `explain`, `replay`, `restore`, `statistics`) are declared `pub mod` in `mod.rs`. Their free functions accept raw `&Connection` (dump.rs:113, restore.rs:200, explain.rs:28, statistics.rs:18, replay.rs:6) without any lock discipline. External callers invoking `memory_engine::inspect::dump::dump_json(conn, ...)` bypass the engine's `with_read`/`write_conn` pool protocol entirely, creating a lock-safety hazard. Verification of callers: every non-test consumer resides in `src/engine/inspect.rs` and `src/engine/restore.rs` (same crate, behind `with_read`). The integration test uses only `memory_engine::inspect::types::*`. No CLI or MCP crate reaches the submodule functions directly. The `pub` visibility is therefore over-broad and misleading.

Current state: `pub mod dump; pub mod explain; pub mod replay; pub mod restore; pub mod statistics;` — all `pub`.
Target state: `pub(crate) mod dump; pub(crate) mod explain; pub(crate) mod replay; pub(crate) mod restore; pub(crate) mod statistics;` — only `types` stays `pub`, re-exported as `pub use types::*`.
Refactoring pattern: Restrict Visibility.
Motivation: encapsulation, lock-safety misuse prevention, cleaner public API surface.
Estimated scope: 1 file (`src/inspect/mod.rs`). Verify no breakage in CLI/MCP crates before committing (confirmed clean by inspection).
Prerequisites: none.
Risk: low — mechanical change, no semantic change.

## Suggested approach
// src/inspect/mod.rs
pub(crate) mod dump;
pub(crate) mod explain;
pub(crate) mod replay;
pub(crate) mod restore;
pub(crate) mod statistics;
pub mod types;

pub use types::*;

```sql
SELECT ... FROM facts
WHERE t_expired IS NOT NULL
  AND t_expired < ?1

ORDER BY id ASC
```

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Dump path security check vulnerable to symlink in final filename component**

- **ID:** `mcp/soundness-dump-path-symlink`
- **Severity:** high
- **Area:** mcp · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `memory-engine-mcp/src/tools/mod.rs:1062-1066`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
The path security check in `handle_dump_state` canonicalizes only the *parent* directory of the client-supplied path. If the final filename component is itself a symlink pointing outside `/tmp` (e.g., `/tmp/escape -> /etc/passwd`), `p.parent()` resolves to `/tmp` (which canonicalizes correctly) while `p` itself still points outside the sandbox. The subsequent `engine.dump_state(&dump_format)` write follows the symlink, enabling arbitrary file overwrite. Additionally, `temp_dir()` is not canonicalized before the `starts_with` comparison: on platforms where `$TMPDIR` or `/tmp` are themselves symlinks (e.g., macOS `/tmp -> /private/tmp`), legitimate paths inside `/private/tmp` fail the check — a false rejection. Both bugs share the same root cause: only one side of the comparison is canonicalized.

## Suggested approach
Canonicalize `p` itself (not just its parent) after creating it: `let canonical = std::fs::canonicalize(&p).map_err(|_| ValidationError::Other(...))?;`. Also canonicalize `temp_dir()` on the right-hand side: `let temp = std::fs::canonicalize(std::env::temp_dir()).unwrap_or_else(|_| std::env::temp_dir());`. This closes both the symlink-filename and the false-rejection bugs. Note that for a non-existent destination file, `canonicalize` will fail; the fix should canonicalize the parent and then reconstruct the full path from the canonicalized parent plus the file_name component.

## References
CWE-59, CWE-22

<!-- super-qa-key: mcp/soundness-dump-path-symlink -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: In-memory graph not updated when commit_archive succeeds but graph.write() is interrupted
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**In-memory graph not updated when commit_archive succeeds but graph.write() is interrupted**

- **ID:** `archive/correctness-graph-state-after-commit`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/engine/archive.rs:82-88`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
After a successful `commit_archive` (facts hard-deleted from SQLite), the code acquires `self.graph.write()` and removes the corresponding nodes and edges. If the process panics or is killed between the SQLite commit and the graph removal loop, the in-memory graph retains stale nodes pointing to facts that no longer exist in the database. On the next engine load the graph is rebuilt from the DB (facts are gone), so persistence survives a restart — but within a single session, any graph query that hits the stale nodes will encounter dangling references. While `parking_lot::RwLock` does not poison, a panic inside the `graph.write()` lock block would drop the lock guard and leave the graph partially pruned.

## Suggested approach
This is inherent to a two-phase commit (SQLite + in-memory). The safest mitigation is to make the graph update loop panic-safe by collecting the fact IDs into a local Vec before entering the lock and wrapping the loop in a catch_unwind guard, or by rebuilding the graph lazily on next access when a missing node is detected.

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Decompression size limit produces opaque serde EOF error, not a clear limit-exceeded error
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Decompression size limit produces opaque serde EOF error, not a clear limit-exceeded error**

- **ID:** `archive/correctness-decompression-bomb-silent-truncation`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/archive/pak.rs:64-65`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`read_pak` applies a 4 GiB cap via `Read::take(decoder, MAX_PAK_DECOMPRESSED_SIZE)`. When a compressed bomb reaches that limit, `take` stops reading and `serde_json::from_reader` receives an unexpected EOF — it returns a `serde_json::Error` with kind `io` ("unexpected end of JSON input"), which is then wrapped as `MemoryError::Serialization`. The caller cannot distinguish between a genuinely truncated/corrupt file and a size-limit trigger. In addition, the 4 GiB default is extremely large — a malicious pak in a test or adversarial restore path would OOM the process long before serde returns an error.

## Suggested approach
After `serde_json::from_reader` returns, verify the reader's position:
```rust
let mut limited = decoder.take(MAX_PAK_DECOMPRESSED_SIZE);
let pak: ArchivePak = serde_json::from_reader(&mut limited)?;
// If we consumed exactly MAX bytes, we likely hit the cap
if limited.limit() == 0 {
    return Err(MemoryError::Archive("pak decompressed size exceeds 4 GiB limit".to_string()));
}
```
Also consider lowering the constant to a realistic maximum (e.g. 256 MiB) given the expected fact payload sizes.

## References
CWE-409: Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification)

**Old fact is read outside the transaction before arbitration (TOCTOU window)**

- **ID:** `conflict/correctness-read-old-fact-outside-tx`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** temporal · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/conflict/temporal.rs:44-45`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`let old_fact = fact_store.get(old_fact_id)?;` runs against the bare `&Connection` BEFORE `conn.unchecked_transaction()?` is opened in the Add/Update/Delete branches (lines 79, 116, 152). Any concurrent writer can mutate `old_fact_id` between the read and the BEGIN, so the arbiter decides on stale data. The Update/Delete branches partially self-heal via `expire_and_invalidate`'s `AND t_expired IS NULL` predicate (which surfaces as `NotFound` if already expired), but other mutations (importance, metadata, valid window) are silently accepted. The Add branch has no such guard and will happily create a `supplements` edge pointing at a fact whose state no longer matches what the arbiter saw.

## Suggested approach
Open the transaction first, then read `old_fact` from a `FactStore::new(&tx, embed_dim)`:

```rust
let tx = conn.unchecked_transaction()?;
let old_fact = FactStore::new(&tx, embed_dim).get(old_fact_id)?;
let decision = arbiter.arbitrate(&old_fact, &new_as_fact)?;
match decision { /* ... */ }
```

This costs one branch of work in the `Noop` case (cheap rollback on drop) but eliminates the read/decide/write race entirely.

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**`conn.unchecked_transaction()` bypasses nested-transaction detection with no documented caller contract**

- **ID:** `conflict/correctness-unchecked-transaction-no-nesting-contract`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** temporal · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/conflict/temporal.rs:79,116,152`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
All three mutation branches call `conn.unchecked_transaction()`. Per rusqlite, this bypasses the `&mut Connection` borrow check that normally prevents nested `BEGIN`s. If `resolve_conflict` is ever invoked from a caller that has already opened a `rusqlite::Transaction` on the same connection (e.g. a future engine-level batch op), SQLite returns `cannot start a transaction within a transaction` at runtime. The function doc says 'all mutations happen in a single transaction' but does not state 'caller must not hold a transaction'. For an embedded library, this is a latent footgun.

## Suggested approach
Either (a) accept `tx: &rusqlite::Transaction<'_>` instead of `conn: &Connection` to make the caller's transaction discipline explicit at the type level, eliminating the need for `unchecked_transaction` entirely; or (b) add an explicit `# Errors` clause stating "the caller must not have an outer transaction open on `conn`; otherwise the inner BEGIN fails at SQLite level." Option (a) is preferred.

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Arithmetic overflow if `from_revision == u16::MAX` in `UpcasterRegistry::register`**

- **ID:** `store/correctness-upcaster-revision-overflow`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/store/upcaster.rs:55`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`let target = from_revision + 1;` at upcaster.rs:55 is plain `u16` addition. If a caller registers an upcaster with `from_revision = u16::MAX` (65535), this panics in debug builds and wraps to 0 in release builds, silently making the `latest` map store revision 0 for the event type. Subsequently, `latest_revision` returns 0, and any stored event at revision 1 would appear 'ahead' of the registry's latest (current_revision >= latest), so the upcasting chain would silently no-op on all events for that type. This is a safe-Rust panic path triggered by an out-of-range API call.

Use checked arithmetic and return an error, or saturate:
```rust
pub fn register(&mut self, event_type: &str, from_revision: u16, func: UpcasterFn) {
    let target = from_revision.checked_add(1)
        .expect("upcaster from_revision u16 overflow — from_revision must be < u16::MAX");
    // ... rest unchanged
}
```
Alternatively, document that `from_revision < u16::MAX` is a precondition and add a debug_assert.

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Full `Fact` struct constructed as scratch pad to call `PersistenceClassifier::should_pin` — redundant 20-field struct allocation repeated per fact**

- **ID:** `bootstrap/design-duplicate-temp-fact-construction`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/bootstrap/mod.rs:207-228`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
In `bootstrap_within_savepoint` (lines 207–228), a complete `crate::types::Fact` is constructed with placeholder values (`id=0`, `content_hash=String::new()`, etc.) solely to call `classifier.should_pin(&temp)`. This is the same pattern used in `engine/ingest.rs:56-79`, but in the bootstrap context the fields `t_valid`, `t_invalid`, `access_count`, `last_accessed` are all set to constants that differ from what `NewFact` will eventually store. The `PersistenceClassifier` trait docs (`traits.rs:87-92`) already document that classifiers should only use `content`, `fact_type`, `importance`, and `metadata`. The current API forces construction of an 11+ field struct when 4 fields matter. A follow-on improvement would be to define a `ClassifierInput<'a>` view type or change `should_pin` to accept `&NewFact` (which holds the same 4 meaningful fields and already exists). Current state: temporary `Fact` struct with ~20 fields, 15 of which are dummy values. Target state: classifier receives `&NewFact` (already exists and has all required fields) so the temp struct is replaced by the already-constructed `new_fact`. Refactoring pattern: Simplify by Reusing Existing Type. Motivation: eliminates allocations, removes confusion about which fields matter, removes the need to keep the temp in sync with `Fact` struct evolution. Scope: `src/bootstrap/mod.rs:206-228` + `src/traits.rs:95` (trait signature) + `src/engine/ingest.rs:56-79` (same pattern). Prerequisites: trait change is semver-breaking. Risk: HIGH — changes `PersistenceClassifier` public trait signature.

## Suggested approach
Change `PersistenceClassifier::should_pin` to accept `&NewFact`:
```rust
pub trait PersistenceClassifier {
    fn should_pin(&self, fact: &NewFact) -> bool { let _ = fact; false }
}
```
Then in `bootstrap_within_savepoint`, build `new_fact` first and call `classifier.should_pin(&new_fact)`, eliminating the temp `Fact` construction entirely.

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Response format detected via if-let chain on `serde_json::Value` instead of typed deserialization**

- **ID:** `embed/design-untyped-response-format`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `memory-engine-embed/src/http.rs:145-158,216-230`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
Current state: Both `embed` and `embed_batch` use untyped `serde_json::Value` with `.get("data")` / `.get("embeddings")` / `.get("embedding")` chains to detect the response format at runtime. The same three-branch detection appears twice (single and batch paths). Target state: Define a `#[derive(Deserialize)] enum EmbeddingResponse { OpenAi { data: Vec<OpenAiItem> }, Ollama { embeddings: Vec<Vec<f32>> }, Direct { embedding: Vec<f32> } }` with `#[serde(untagged)]`, deserialize once with `serde_json::from_value`, then match on the enum variant. This eliminates manual field probing, provides compile-checked field names, centralises the format knowledge, and removes the need for the redundant `.clone()` calls on individual array elements. Refactoring pattern: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism / introduce typed deserialization. Motivation: readability, correctness (typos in string keys become compile errors), coupling (format knowledge in one place). Estimated scope: 1 file. Prerequisites: add `serde` derive to the crate (already available transitively via `memory-engine` dep). Risk: low–medium — `#[serde(untagged)]` disambiguation must be tested against all three server fixtures.

## Suggested approach
#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
struct OpenAiItem {
    index: Option<usize>,
    embedding: Vec<f32>,
}

#[derive(serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(untagged)]
enum EmbeddingResponse {
    OpenAi { data: Vec<OpenAiItem> },
    Ollama { embeddings: Vec<Vec<f32>> },
    Direct { embedding: Vec<f32> },
}

// Then in embed():
let resp_body: EmbeddingResponse = resp.json()
    .map_err(|e| MemoryError::Internal(format!("...")))?;
match resp_body {
    EmbeddingResponse::OpenAi { data } => data.into_iter().next()
        .map(|i| i.embedding)
        .ok_or_else(|| MemoryError::Internal("empty data array".into())),
    EmbeddingResponse::Ollama { embeddings } => embeddings.into_iter().next()
        .ok_or_else(|| MemoryError::Internal("empty embeddings array".into())),
    EmbeddingResponse::Direct { embedding } => Ok(embedding),
}

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**JSON object header hand-assembled with raw `write!` instead of a structured serializer — schema contract held only by a test**

- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/inspect/dump.rs:43-73`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`stream_snapshot` at line 43 manually constructs the JSON object header:
```rust
write!(writer, r#"{{"schema_version":{schema_version},"storage_epoch":{storage_epoch},"embed_dim":{embed_dim}"#)?;
```
and then calls `stream_for_each` for each collection. The field names and order are duplicated relative to `EngineSnapshot`'s serde-derived representation. If `EngineSnapshot` fields are renamed or reordered (e.g., a new top-level scalar is added for Phase 5), the streaming path silently diverges. The only thing preventing a mismatch is the `streaming_output_matches_snapshot_schema` test at dump.rs:278 — a test, not a compile-time constraint.

A fully type-safe streaming approach would use `serde_json::Serializer` with `serialize_map` for the object root, serializing scalar fields normally and collections via `stream_for_each`. Alternatively, a `SnapshotHeader { schema_version, storage_epoch, embed_dim, config }` struct carrying only scalars could be fully serde-serialized, with collections streamed afterwards — but this requires changing the JSON structure.

Current state: raw `write!` macro assembles JSON field names.
Target state: use serde's `Serializer`/`serialize_map` API so field names track the struct definition.
Refactoring pattern: Replace Hand-Rolled Serialization with Library Serializer.
Motivation: correctness, schema evolution safety.
Estimated scope: `src/inspect/dump.rs` only; restore.rs and the snapshot format are unchanged.
Prerequisites: familiarity with `serde_json::ser::Serializer`.
Risk: medium — the streaming guarantee (O(1) peak memory) must be preserved; the serde map API supports this but requires care.

## Suggested approach

use serde::ser::SerializeMap;
let mut ser = serde_json::Serializer::new(&mut *writer);
let mut map = ser.serialize_map(None)?;
map.serialize_entry("schema_version", &schema_version)?;
map.serialize_entry("storage_epoch", &storage_epoch)?;
map.serialize_entry("embed_dim", &embed_dim)?;

Prerequisites: existing test suite covers both paths.
Risk: low — mechanical substitution, no external API change (pool is pub(crate)).

    FileBacked { read_pool_size: usize },
    InMemory,
}

    match self.mode {
        BackendMode::InMemory => ReadConn::InMemory(WriteAsReadGuard { guard: self.write_conn.lock() }),
        BackendMode::FileBacked { .. } => { /* Condvar pop path */ }

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**WriteAsReadGuard name implies read-only but exposes a fully-writable Connection with no query_only PRAGMA**

- **ID:** `pool/design-writeasreadguard-semantics`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/pool/connection_pool.rs:52-60`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
Current state: `WriteAsReadGuard<'a>` (line 52-60) wraps the `write_conn` `MutexGuard` and implements `Deref<Target = Connection>`. The name suggests read-only semantics, but the underlying connection was opened with full read-write privileges and no `PRAGMA query_only = ON` is applied in the in-memory path. A caller receiving a `ReadConn::InMemory(guard)` via `pool.read()` can execute `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` statements through it without any Rust-level or SQLite-level prevention.

By contrast, the file-backed read connections in `open()` explicitly set `PRAGMA query_only = ON` (line 101-102), enforcing read-only at the SQLite level.

Target state: either (a) apply `PRAGMA query_only = ON` to in-memory connections used for read paths (not possible without a separate connection), or (b) rename `WriteAsReadGuard` to `SharedWriteGuard` or `SerializedReadGuard` to accurately reflect that it is a serialized-read-through-write-conn wrapper, not a read-only guard, and update docs accordingly.

Refactoring pattern: Rename to match semantics; optionally add enforcement.
Motivation: readability, correctness (misuse-resistance).
Estimated scope: 1 struct rename + doc update in `connection_pool.rs`.
Prerequisites: none.
Risk: zero for rename; medium for adding a separate read-only in-memory connection.

## Suggested approach
// Option (b): rename to make semantics explicit
pub struct SerializedReadGuard<'a> {
    guard: MutexGuard<'a, Connection>,
}

pub enum ReadConn<'a> {
    Pooled(ReadGuard<'a>),
    InMemory(SerializedReadGuard<'a>),  // write conn reused, no query_only
}

**Documented pipeline order is wrong: marker event ingested first, not last**

- **ID:** `bootstrap/documentation-pipeline-order`

- **Location:** `src/bootstrap/mod.rs:3-4, src/bootstrap/mod.rs:32-33`

## Description
Both the module-level doc comment (lines 3-4) and the `bootstrap_session_inner` doc (lines 32-33) describe the pipeline as: `parse → reconstruct turns → classify outcome → keyword pre-filter → extract facts → ingest marker event + add facts`. Change both doc strings to:
```

//! → reconstruct turns → classify outcome → keyword pre-filter → extract facts → add facts.
```

**`BootstrapConfig::max_turns` doc omits tail-selection semantics**

- **ID:** `bootstrap/documentation-max-turns-tail-semantics`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** docs
- **Location:** `src/bootstrap/metrics.rs:10-11`

## Description
The field doc says only "Maximum turns to process per session. `0` = no limit." The actual behaviour in `bootstrap_within_savepoint` (mod.rs:162-166) is that when the turn count exceeds `max_turns`, the TAIL (most recent turns) is kept — not the head. This is a deliberate design decision (outcome evidence lives at session end), documented only in an inline comment. Public field docs don't surface this, so consumers who expect head-truncation will be surprised.

## Suggested approach
```rust
/// Maximum turns to process per session. `0` = no limit.
///
/// When the session exceeds this limit the **most-recent** turns are kept
/// (tail selection), because outcome evidence — commits, test results —
/// concentrates at the end of sessions. Outcome classification always runs
/// on the full turn list before truncation.
pub max_turns: usize,
```

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**resolve_conflict doc omits synthetic-fact caveat for ConflictArbiter implementers**

- **ID:** `conflict/documentation-synthetic-fact-caveat`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** temporal · **Type:** docs
- **Location:** `src/conflict/temporal.rs:18-34 (resolve_conflict doc) and lines 47-67 (new_as_fact construction)`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
The public doc-comment for `resolve_conflict` (lines 18–34) describes each `CrudDecision` branch but never warns `ConflictArbiter` implementers that the `new_fact` argument they receive inside `arbitrate` is a pre-insert synthetic. Concretely, two fields diverge from the eventually-stored values: `id` is hardcoded to 0 (placeholder, not yet inserted, line 49) and `importance_score` is hardcoded to 0.5 (line 65) regardless of `new_fact.importance`, whereas `FactStore::insert` (store/facts.rs:95) seeds `importance_score` from `fact.importance`. An arbiter that reads `new_fact.id` for cross-referencing or `new_fact.importance_score` for ranking will silently get wrong data. The analogous warning already exists in traits.rs:87–92 for `PersistenceClassifier::should_pin` ('The Fact passed … is a pre-insert synthetic with id=0 … Classifiers should only rely on content, fact_type, importance …') but is absent from the call-site where the same constraint applies to the arbiter.

## Suggested approach
Add a doc caveat on `resolve_conflict` (and consider mirroring it on `ConflictArbiter::arbitrate` in traits.rs) modelled on the PersistenceClassifier caveat at traits.rs:87–92:

```rust
/// **Arbiter input caveat:** The `new_fact` passed to [`ConflictArbiter::arbitrate`] is a
/// pre-insert synthetic: `id` is always 0 (not yet assigned by the database) and
/// `importance_score` is seeded to 0.5 rather than `new_fact.importance`.
/// Arbiters must not rely on `id` or `importance_score`; use `content`, `fact_type`,
/// `importance`, and `metadata` instead.
```

Optionally, also fix the hardcode on line 65 to `importance_score: new_fact.importance` so that the synthetic value matches storage semantics (store/facts.rs:95 already seeds it this way), making the caveat narrower (id-only).

## References
src/conflict/temporal.rs:18-34, src/conflict/temporal.rs:49, src/conflict/temporal.rs:65, src/traits.rs:87-92, src/store/facts.rs:95

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**`ebbinghaus_decay` is `pub` but documents no precondition on `half_life`**

- **ID:** `forgetting/documentation-ebbinghaus-precondition`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** forgetting · **Type:** docs
- **Location:** `src/forgetting/policy.rs:18-24`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`ebbinghaus_decay(age_days, half_life)` is a public, `#[must_use]` function. When called with `half_life = 0.0` and `age_days = 0.0`, Rust IEEE 754 evaluates `-0.0/0.0 = NaN`, so `f64::exp2(NaN) = NaN`. With `half_life = 0.0` and any positive `age_days`, the result is `0.0` (not a panic, but semantically wrong — immediate full forgetting). With a negative `half_life`, the result exceeds 1.0, violating the stated `[0,1]` contract. The doc comment says nothing about these edge cases. The guard (`policy.validate()` in `prune`) is only on the `prune` call path; direct callers of the public function get silent wrong values. Confirmed empirically: `ebbinghaus_decay(0.0, 0.0)` returns `NaN` in Rust.

## Suggested approach
Add a `# Panics` (or `# Note`) section:
```rust
/// # Note
///
/// `half_life` must be positive and finite. Passing `half_life <= 0.0`
/// or `NaN` produces `NaN` or values outside `[0, 1]` without panicking.
/// When called through [`prune`], this is guaranteed by [`ForgetPolicy::validate`].
/// Direct callers are responsible for satisfying this precondition.
```

## References
—

<!-- super-qa-key: forgetting/documentation-ebbinghaus-precondition -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Consumer traits lack Send + Sync supertrait bounds while async wrappers mandate them
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Consumer traits lack Send + Sync supertrait bounds while async wrappers mandate them**

- **ID:** `core-root/modern-rust-consumer-trait-send-sync-asymmetry`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/traits.rs:11,43,60,93,149,167`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
Only `Reranker` (traits.rs:124) carries `: Send + Sync`. The other five consumer traits — EmbeddingProvider (l.11), SummaryGenerator (l.43), ConflictArbiter (l.60), PersistenceClassifier (l.93), InsightStream (l.149), DreamCycle (l.167) — do not. This forces every async_engine.rs call-site to repeat `+ Send + Sync` in the concrete bound (async_engine.rs:102, 103, 125, 126, 164, 184, 524, 537), and consumers must annotate all their `Arc<dyn Trait>` usages with the compound bound. The disparity is not intentional (there is no doc comment explaining it) and creates an API surface inconsistency: the trait definition under-constrains while every practical usage over-constrains.

## Suggested approach
Add `: Send + Sync` to all five traits that are consumed through async wrappers:

```rust
pub trait EmbeddingProvider: Send + Sync { ... }
pub trait SummaryGenerator: Send + Sync { ... }
pub trait ConflictArbiter: Send + Sync { ... }
pub trait PersistenceClassifier: Send + Sync { ... }
pub trait InsightStream: Send + Sync { ... }
pub trait DreamCycle: Send + Sync { ... }
```

Async call-sites can then drop the redundant `+ Send + Sync` from their `Arc<dyn Trait + Send + Sync>` parameters.

## References
—

<!-- super-qa-key: core-root/modern-rust-consumer-trait-send-sync-asymmetry -->

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Active facts loaded twice from SQLite within a single consolidation run
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Active facts loaded twice from SQLite within a single consolidation run**

- **ID:** `consolidation/correctness-dedup-cluster-double-table-scan`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** consolidation · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/consolidation/dedup.rs:34, src/consolidation/cluster.rs:39`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`local_dedup` calls `fact_store.list_active(None)` (dedup.rs:34) and then `cluster_fusion` calls `fact_store.list_active(None)` again (cluster.rs:39), both within the same transaction. Each call deserializes every active fact's embedding BLOB from SQLite into a `Vec<f32>`. For a corpus of 50 000 facts with 768-dimension embeddings this is ~147 MB of data processed twice — ~294 MB per consolidation run — before reaching the 50 000-fact safety cap. The two separate queries are intentional in that cluster sees the post-dedup state, but the second load still incurs the full deserialization cost.

## Suggested approach
Pass the already-loaded `active_facts: Vec<Fact>` from `local_dedup`'s result (possibly as a separate return element) into `cluster_fusion` so it can filter expired IDs and avoid re-loading. Alternatively, make the orchestrator responsible for loading facts once and passing the slice into each pass. This requires adjusting the function signatures but removes the redundant scan.

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: N+1 individual UPDATE statements for importance_score materialization
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**N+1 individual UPDATE statements for importance_score materialization**

- **ID:** `forgetting/perf-n-plus-one-score-update`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** forgetting · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/forgetting/policy.rs:114-118`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`update_importance_score` (store/facts.rs:564-570) executes one `UPDATE facts SET importance_score = ?1 WHERE id = ?2` per active fact inside the transaction. For a store with 100k facts this issues 100k individual prepared-statement executions. SQLite batches writes within a transaction efficiently, but each call still incurs statement preparation overhead and a B-tree write per row. A single bulk UPDATE via `json_each` would collapse this to one statement regardless of corpus size.

## Suggested approach
Add a `update_importance_scores_bulk(scores: &[(i64, f64)])` method to `FactStore` using `json_each`:
```sql
UPDATE facts
SET importance_score = (
    SELECT value
    FROM json_each(?1)
    WHERE key = CAST(facts.id AS TEXT)
)
WHERE id IN (SELECT key FROM json_each(?1))
```
Or use a temporary table approach for very large datasets. Call this once from `prune` with the full scored vec instead of looping `update_importance_score`.

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: list_active deserializes embedding BLOBs and metadata JSON that prune never uses
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**list_active deserializes embedding BLOBs and metadata JSON that prune never uses**

- **ID:** `forgetting/perf-wasteful-embedding-deserialize`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** forgetting · **Type:** refactor
- **Location:** `src/forgetting/policy.rs:92`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`prune` calls `fact_store.list_active(None)` which routes through `row_to_fact` (store/facts.rs:815). That function always deserializes the `embedding` BLOB into `Vec<f32>` (line 837, up to 3 072 bytes for a 768-dim embedding) and the `metadata` TEXT into `serde_json::Value` (line 841) for every active fact. `compute_importance` uses none of these fields — it only reads `fact.id`, `fact.fact_type`, `fact.last_accessed`, `fact.access_count`, `fact.importance`, and `fact.is_pinned`. On a store with 100k facts at 768 dimensions, the prune pass allocates ~300 MB of embedding heap data it immediately discards.

## Suggested approach
Add a lightweight scoring projection to `FactStore`:
```rust
pub struct ScoringFact {
    pub id: i64,
    pub fact_type: FactType,
    pub last_accessed: DateTime<Utc>,
    pub access_count: i64,
    pub importance: f64,
    pub is_pinned: bool,
}

pub fn list_active_for_scoring(&self) -> Result<Vec<ScoringFact>> {
    // SELECT id, fact_type, last_accessed, access_count, importance, is_pinned
    // FROM facts WHERE t_expired IS NULL
```

## Description
compute_statistics fires 10 separate query_row calls: 5 against facts (lines 23, 24-28, 29-33, 34-38, 40-44), 3 against edges (lines 47, 48-52, 53-57), 2 against scopes (82-86), 1 against events (89), plus 1 prepared GROUP BY statement for summaries. **Tier-3 (due) fetches all due facts unbounded, deserializes embeddings, then filters and caps in Rust**

- **ID:** `resume/perf-due-no-sql-limit`

- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
At context.rs:93-98 the resume layer calls `fact_store.list_due(config.now, scope_ids)` — which has no `LIMIT` clause and no exclusion of already-seen IDs (facts.rs:397-427) — then applies `.filter(|f| !seen.contains(&f.id)).take(config.due_cap)` in Rust. Align Tier 3 with Tiers 2 and 4: pass `due_cap` and the current `seen` set into an updated `list_due` API so the SQL layer applies `AND id NOT IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(?)) … LIMIT ?`. Until the store API is extended, a short-circuit at the resume layer avoids the worst case:
```rust
let due: Vec<Fact> = fact_store
    .list_due(config.now, scope_ids)?
    .into_iter()
    .filter(|f| !seen.contains(&f.id))
    .take(config.due_cap)
    .collect();
```
The structural fix is to add `exclude: &HashSet<i64>, limit: usize` parameters to `FactStore::list_due` and push them to SQL, matching `list_by_importance_score`'s pattern.

**Manual NewFact→Fact field-copy should be a From impl or constructor**

- **ID:** `conflict/refactoring-manual-newfact-to-fact`
- **Severity:** medium

## Description
Current state: a 19-line block inside `resolve_conflict` manually copies every field of `new_fact: &NewFact` into a heap-allocated `crate::types::Fact`, with two hardcoded values (`id: 0` placeholder and `importance_score: 0.5`). The `importance_score` is silently pinned to 0.5 regardless of `new_fact.importance`, so an arbiter inspecting `new_fact.importance_score` sees the wrong value—potentially causing wrong decisions. Target state: add `impl From<&NewFact> for Fact` (or a `Fact::from_new_for_arbiter(nf: &NewFact) -> Fact`) in `types.rs` that seeds `importance_score` from `nf.importance` (the closest approximation before insertion). Then the 19-line block collapses to one line. Refactoring pattern: Extract Constructor / Introduce Conversion Trait. Motivation: readability, misuse-resistance (the arbiter silent-wrong-value bug), and single point of change when `Fact` gains new fields—today any future field added to `Fact` must also be added to this manual block or it silently defaults. Estimated scope: 2 files (`types.rs` for the impl, `temporal.rs` for the call site). Prerequisites: confirm the arbiter contract (only `content`, `fact_type`, `importance`, `metadata` are stable; `id`, `scope_id`, `importance_score`, `access_count` are explicitly unstable per `PersistenceClassifier` doc—that warning is absent from `ConflictArbiter`). Risk: LOW—purely mechanical after the From impl is added; no behavior change if `importance_score` is seeded from `importance` (which is the documented intent). HEAVY: requires human judgement on the `importance_score` seeding choice.

## Suggested approach
// types.rs
impl Fact {
    /// Construct a transient `Fact` from a `NewFact` for passing to `ConflictArbiter::arbitrate`.
    /// `id` is 0 (not yet assigned), `importance_score` is seeded from `importance`.
    pub(crate) fn from_new_for_arbiter(nf: &NewFact) -> Self {
        Self {
            id: 0,
            content: nf.content.clone(),
            content_hash: nf.content_hash.clone(),
            embedding: nf.embedding.clone(),
            fact_type: nf.fact_type.clone(),
            t_created: nf.t_created,
            t_expired: nf.t_expired,
            t_valid: nf.t_valid,
            t_invalid: nf.t_invalid,
            source_event_id: nf.source_event_id,
            scope_id: nf.scope_id,
            importance: nf.importance,
            access_count: nf.access_count,
            last_accessed: nf.last_accessed,
            metadata: nf.metadata.clone(),
            is_pinned: nf.is_pinned,
            importance_score: nf.importance, // best approximation before insertion
            surfaced_at: None,
        }
    }
}
// temporal.rs line 48-67 replaced by:
let new_as_fact = crate::types::Fact::from_new_for_arbiter(new_fact);

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis (security lens ran via octo tier-2 fallback, xhigh not effort:max); **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Quadratic-time turn reconstruction amplifies parse DoS into CPU exhaustion**

- **ID:** `bootstrap/dos-quadratic-turn-reconstruction`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** security
- **Location:** `src/bootstrap/filter.rs:114,151`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
reconstruct_turns runs two O(n^2) scans over the attacker-controlled `relevant` entry slice. The UUID-linked pass (filter.rs:102-136) calls `relevant.iter().find(...)` once per user entry (filter.rs:114), and the sequential-fallback pass (filter.rs:141-174) does `relevant[i+1..].iter().take_while(...).find(...)` per user entry (filter.rs:151). For a session of N user entries with no matching assistant replies, both passes scan ~N elements N times -> ~N^2/2 comparisons. Combined with the unbounded entry count (see bootstrap/dos-unbounded-parse-allocation), a few-hundred-MB file of unpaired user entries yields billions of string comparisons, pinning a CPU core for an extended period (algorithmic-complexity DoS). collect_tool_result_entries (filter.rs:217-233) adds a further linear scan per call inside the per-user loop, compounding it.

## Suggested approach
Pre-index assistants for O(1) lookup so pairing is O(n). Before the loops, build `let mut by_parent: HashMap<&str, &SessionEntry> = HashMap::new();` mapping `assistant.parent_uuid -> assistant` (and a separate index of tool-result entries keyed by their `parent_uuid`). Replace the inner `.find()` at filter.rs:114 with `by_parent.get(user_uuid.as_str())`, and replace the linear scan in collect_tool_result_entries with a lookup into the tool-result index. This reduces total work to O(n). Independently, capping MAX_ENTRIES (per the parse fix) bounds the worst case even if the algorithm is left quadratic.

CWE-407, CWE-400, CWE-1333

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Unbounded full-document JSON parse of attacker-controlled snapshot to read one field
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis (security lens ran via octo tier-2 fallback, xhigh not effort:max); **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Unbounded full-document JSON parse of attacker-controlled snapshot to read one field**

- **ID:** `cli/dos-import-header-unbounded-parse`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** cli · **Type:** security
- **Location:** `memory-engine-cli/src/commands/import.rs:49-55`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`peek_embed_dim` wraps the snapshot file in a `BufReader` and calls `serde_json::from_reader::<SnapshotHeader>(reader)` to extract a single `embed_dim: usize`. serde_json does not stop after the known field — it tokenizes and validates the ENTIRE JSON document up to EOF, allocating intermediate `String`/buffer storage for arbitrarily large object keys and values. There is no `.take(N)` byte cap on the reader. The snapshot file is the import source, i.e. fully attacker-controlled input (the trust boundary). This runs only on the plain-JSON path (when `--embed-dim` is omitted), but in that case a multi-GB or pathological header drives unbounded memory allocation before `restore_json` (which the inspect-module audit notes has its own 4 GiB cap) is ever reached. This is a redundant, uncapped pre-parse introduced by the CLI itself, separate from the engine's restore path. serde_json's default 128-deep recursion limit bounds the nesting/stack-overflow vector but NOT total width/bytes. CWE-400, CWE-770.

## Suggested approach
Cap the bytes fed to the header parser, e.g.:

    use std::io::Read;
    const MAX_HEADER_BYTES: u64 = 1 << 20; // 1 MiB is ample for a JSON header object
    let file = std::fs::File::open(path)?;
    let reader = std::io::BufReader::new(file).take(MAX_HEADER_BYTES);
    let header: SnapshotHeader = serde_json::from_reader(reader)
        .map_err(|e| anyhow::anyhow!("failed to read snapshot header (>1MiB or malformed): {e}"))?;

Better still, use `serde_json::Deserializer::from_reader(reader).into_iter::<SnapshotHeader>().next()` over the capped reader so the parser stops at the first complete value instead of requiring clean EOF.

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis (security lens ran via octo tier-2 fallback, xhigh not effort:max); **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**SQLite write transaction held open across consumer LLM/network calls (DoS / lock starvation)**

- **ID:** `consolidation/dos-lock-held-across-llm-io`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** consolidation · **Type:** security
- **Location:** `src/consolidation/mod.rs:50; src/consolidation/cluster.rs:70-71; src/consolidation/global.rs:59-60`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
consolidate() opens a single write transaction at mod.rs:50 (conn.unchecked_transaction()) and keeps it open for the entire 3-pass pipeline. Inside that transaction, cluster_fusion calls generator.summarize(&cluster_facts)? and generator.embed(&summary_text)? (cluster.rs:70-71), and global_integration does the same (global.rs:59-60). Per the crate's own design contract, SummaryGenerator delegates ALL LLM/network work to the consumer, so these are unbounded-latency network round-trips. The SQLite write lock is held for the full duration. The engine wraps its write connection in a Mutex (verified: src/engine/mod.rs:508 `fn write_conn(&self) -> Result<MutexGuard<'_, Connection>>`), so a slow, timing-out, or hanging consumer endpoint serializes and stalls the entire engine's write path — every concurrent writer blocks for the round-trip duration. WAL mode keeps readers alive but does not help writers. A consumer with N clusters makes N sequential blocking network calls under the lock. This is the only finding in scope with a real availability attack surface.

## Suggested approach
Do not hold the write transaction across consumer trait calls. Restructure each pass to: (1) read fact/summary inputs under a short read scope, (2) drop the lock and invoke generator.summarize/embed with no transaction held, (3) re-acquire and open a short write transaction only to insert the produced summaries. Example for cluster_fusion: collect all (cluster_facts, source_ids, scope_id) first, release the tx, run all summarize/embed calls, then open a fresh tx for the batch of summary_store.insert(...) calls. Optionally document a consumer-side timeout requirement on SummaryGenerator. Note this trades the current single-transaction atomicity for per-batch atomicity — acceptable since consolidation is idempotent (delete_by_level + rebuild).

## References
CWE-400, CWE-833, CWE-667

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Unbounded HTTP response body read into memory (no size cap) — resource-exhaustion DoS
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis (security lens ran via octo tier-2 fallback, xhigh not effort:max); **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Unbounded HTTP response body read into memory (no size cap) — resource-exhaustion DoS**

- **ID:** `embed/dos-unbounded-response-body`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** security
- **Location:** `memory-engine-embed/src/http.rs:132,138,203,209`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
Both embed() and embed_batch() consume the full HTTP response with `resp.json()` (lines 138, 209) and, on the error path, `resp.text()` (lines 132, 203). reqwest::blocking::Response::json()/text() buffer the entire body into memory with no length limit. A compromised, buggy, or misconfigured endpoint (e.g. a URL accidentally pointed at a large HTML page or an adversarial server streaming gigabytes) causes unbounded allocation and can OOM the host agent. There is a timeout on the client (good) but no body-size cap, and a slow-trickle large body can stay under the timeout while exhausting memory. This is the only crate in the workspace with a live network dependency, so this is the primary inbound-network resource-exhaustion vector.

## Suggested approach
Add a configurable max-body cap. Check `resp.content_length()` against a limit before consuming, and/or read with a bounded reader instead of `.json()`:
    const MAX_BODY: u64 = 32 * 1024 * 1024;
    if let Some(len) = resp.content_length() { if len > MAX_BODY { return Err(MemoryError::Internal(format!("embedding response too large: {len} bytes"))); } }
    let bytes = resp.bytes().map_err(...)?; // still bounded by client config
    if bytes.len() as u64 > MAX_BODY { return Err(...); }
    let body: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_slice(&bytes).map_err(...)?;
Content-Length can be absent/lied about, so also enforce the cap on the actually-read byte count.

## Description
`load_from_file()` reads the entire `.snapshot` sidecar into memory with `fs::read(path)` (line 210, no size cap) and then deserializes the payload with `rmp_serde::from_slice` (line 277) into `SnapshotPayload`, which contains `Vec<GraphEdgeSnapshot>`, `Vec<ScopeNode>`, and `Vec<HnswEntry>` (each `HnswEntry` holding a `Vec<f32>` embedding). rmp-serde 1.3.1 honors the MessagePack array-length prefix via serde's `size_hint`, so the derived `Visitor` performs `Vec::with_capacity(declared_len)` BEFORE consuming elements. A crafted file that declares a huge array length forces a large up-front allocation (memory-exhaustion / OOM-abort DoS) even though the file itself is small.

The blake3 checksum (verified at line 270, before payload deserialize at 277) is the only gate, but blake3 here is UNKEYED and serves as a corruption/integrity check, not an authentication control: any actor able to write the sidecar can recompute a matching blake3 over a malicious payload. The header is deserialized at line 241 BEFORE the checksum check, but `SnapshotHeader` holds only scalar fields, so the amplification risk is confined to the payload path.

Threat model: exploitation requires write access to the `<db>.snapshot` file in the engine's own data directory, so this is a local tamper / shared-data-dir DoS rather than a remote one — hence medium, not high. The flat (non-recursive) snapshot types mean there is no stack-overflow/recursion-depth angle here; the concern is purely unbounded allocation. CWE-502, CWE-400, CWE-789.

## Suggested approach
Cap both the file size and the per-collection element counts before/while deserializing. Minimal mechanical guard at the file level:

```rust
const MAX_SNAPSHOT_BYTES: u64 = 512 * 1024 * 1024; // tune to expected corpus
let meta = fs::metadata(path).ok()?;
if meta.len() > MAX_SNAPSHOT_BYTES {
    tracing::warn!(path = %path.display(), size = meta.len(), "snapshot exceeds size cap, discarding");
    return None;
}
let data = fs::read(path).ok()?; // already capped
```

The robust fix additionally bounds the in-band declared lengths so a small file cannot pre-allocate a huge Vec: deserialize through a length-limited reader/visitor, or post-validate `payload.graph.edges.len()`, `payload.scope_tree.nodes.len()`, and each `HnswEntry::embedding.len() == embed_dim` (the embedding-dim check already exists in ann.rs:191 but only on the ann load path). Because blake3 is unkeyed it cannot be relied on as an authenticity gate; if sidecar authenticity matters, use a keyed MAC (blake3::keyed_hash) with a key not stored beside the file.

## References
CWE-502, CWE-400, CWE-789

<!-- super-qa-key: engine/security-snapshot-unbounded-deserialize -->

[super-qa] medium: memory_dump_state path guard follows symlinks on leaf and has a check-to-use (TOCTOU) window
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis (security lens ran via octo tier-2 fallback, xhigh not effort:max); **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**memory_dump_state path guard follows symlinks on leaf and has a check-to-use (TOCTOU) window**

- **ID:** `mcp/path-dumpstate-symlink-toctou`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** mcp · **Type:** security
- **Location:** `memory-engine-mcp/src/tools/mod.rs:1056-1079 (handle_dump_state path guard)`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
The guard canonicalizes the PARENT directory and checks canonical.starts_with(temp_dir()). Canonicalizing the parent correctly defeats '..' traversal (this is stronger than a lexical starts_with check). However: (1) the leaf filename component is never canonicalized, so if an attacker who can write to the temp dir places a symlink there (e.g. /tmp/x -> /home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys), the downstream File::create / fs::rename in src/inspect/dump.rs:115,119 follows it and writes engine-snapshot JSON outside the temp jail (CWE-59). (2) There is a TOCTOU gap between std::fs::canonicalize(parent) here and the later File::create/rename in dump.rs — the parent (or a path component) can be swapped after the check (CWE-367). Practical severity is bounded by the precondition of prior write access to the temp directory, and the written content is a memory snapshot rather than fully attacker-chosen bytes. Note: std::env::temp_dir() also honors TMPDIR/TMP/TEMP, but those are operator launch-time env, not client-controllable over JSON-RPC, so they are not part of this finding.

## Suggested approach
Resolve and reject symlinks on the full target and create atomically. Canonicalize the leaf if it exists and re-check containment; create the dump via tempfile::NamedTempFile in the temp dir then persist, or open the destination with OpenOptions::new().write(true).create_new(true).custom_flags(libc::O_NOFOLLOW) so an existing symlink leaf fails. Simplest robust fix: ignore the client-supplied directory entirely and always write to a freshly minted tempfile::Builder path inside std::env::temp_dir(), returning the generated path — the client does not need to choose the location.

## References
CWE-59, CWE-367, CWE-22

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Unbounded read_pool_size leads to FD exhaustion / large allocation (CWE-770/789)
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis (security lens ran via octo tier-2 fallback, xhigh not effort:max); **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Unbounded read_pool_size leads to FD exhaustion / large allocation (CWE-770/789)**

- **ID:** `pool/resource-exhaustion-unbounded-read-pool-size`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** security
- **Location:** `src/pool/connection_pool.rs:98-104 (also 166-170)`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`ConnectionPool::open` and `open_read_only` take `read_pool_size: usize` directly from the consumer-facing `EngineConfig.read_pool_size` (a `pub usize` field in src/engine/mod.rs:63 with no upper-bound validation). It flows unchecked into `Vec::with_capacity(read_pool_size)` (line 98 / 166) and a `for _ in 0..read_pool_size` loop that opens that many SQLite connections (lines 99-104 / 167-170). A large value (e.g. millions, or usize::MAX) attempts an oversized capacity reservation and/or exhausts the process file-descriptor table, each open being a real OS handle. This is consumer-controlled rather than network-attacker-controlled (embedded in-process library), which bounds the severity, but there is no defensive cap and no error returned before resource pressure. CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits), CWE-789 (Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value).

## Suggested approach
Clamp at the pool boundary so the invariant is enforced regardless of caller: `const MAX_READ_POOL: usize = 256; let read_pool_size = read_pool_size.min(MAX_READ_POOL);` before `Vec::with_capacity(...)`. Alternatively return `MemoryError` for values above the cap so the misconfiguration is surfaced rather than silently clamped. Apply identically in `open` and `open_read_only`.

## References
CWE-770, CWE-789

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: pub write() bypasses the read-only guard enforced by try_write()
manifest.body:
> ✅ **Verified against primary source.** VERIFIED: query_only=ON backstops write_conn in RO pool + callers use writable pools — defense-in-depth footgun, not live vuln

**pub write() bypasses the read-only guard enforced by try_write()**

- **ID:** `pool/soundness-write-bypasses-readonly-guard`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/pool/connection_pool.rs:206-208`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
ConnectionPool::write() (line 206) locks and returns the write connection unconditionally with no check on self.read_only. ConnectionPool::try_write() (line 213-218) is the only method that enforces the ReadOnly invariant. Because write() is pub, any caller that reaches the pool directly — rather than through the engine's write_conn() helper — can acquire a mutable connection on a database that was opened with SQLITE_OPEN_READ_ONLY flags, causing an SQLite error at execution time instead of a clean MemoryError::ReadOnly. Today engine/restore.rs lines 55 and 84 call pool.write() directly without checking is_read_only() first. If restore paths ever become reachable on a read-only engine the SQLite-level error will surface rather than the typed error.

## Suggested approach
Restrict write() to pub(crate) so only internal engine code can call it, and route all write access through try_write() (or write_conn()). Alternatively, make write() return Result<MutexGuard<'_, Connection>, MemoryError> with the same read_only guard:

```rust
// pub(crate) — kills the external footgun entirely
pub(crate) fn write(&self) -> MutexGuard<'_, Connection> {
    self.write_conn.lock()
}
```
Or merge write() and try_write() into a single pub fn that always checks:
```rust
pub fn write(&self) -> Result<MutexGuard<'_, Connection>> {
    if self.read_only {
        return Err(MemoryError::ReadOnly);
    }
    Ok(self.write_conn.lock())
}
```
Update restore.rs callers accordingly.

## References
CWE-732, CWE-284

manifest.title: [super-qa] medium: Post-commit graph mutation creates a split-brain window if a panic occurs between DB commit and graph update
manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Post-commit graph mutation creates a split-brain window if a panic occurs between DB commit and graph update**

- **ID:** `conflict/soundness-graph-db-split-brain`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** temporal · **Type:** bug
- **Location:** `src/conflict/temporal.rs:95-112,139-148,160-164`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
In all three mutation branches, `tx.commit()?` succeeds first, then the in-memory `MemoryGraph` is mutated (e.g. `graph.add_edge(...)`, `graph.remove_edges_by_fact(...)`). A panic between the commit and the graph mutation leaves the DB and graph diverged for the rest of the session. The engine recovers on the next `open()` via `MemoryGraph::load_from_db`, but within-session query results (graph neighbors, degree-based importance scoring) will be wrong. This is a safe-Rust soundness concern: no invariant in the type system prevents the partial state.

## Suggested approach
Document the invariant explicitly in the function doc and in `MemoryGraph` that the graph is eventually consistent, recovered on `open()`. Longer-term: consider a two-phase approach where the graph is updated speculatively before commit and rolled back on `tx.commit()` failure, trading the split-brain from the post-commit panic window (rare) for a pre-commit rollback (reliable). Alternatively, validate with `debug_assert!(graph_and_db_consistent())` in tests to catch drift early.

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Watermark suppression when dedup is skipped (usize::MAX sentinel) has no integration test**

- **ID:** `consolidation/testing-no-watermark-suppression-integration-test`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** consolidation · **Type:** test
- **Location:** `src/consolidation/mod.rs:55-66`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
When `local_dedup` returns `usize::MAX` (over-cap path, dedup.rs:45), `consolidate()` must NOT advance `last_consolidated_at` so skipped facts are retried later. This logic (mod.rs:55-66) is critical for correctness: if the watermark were advanced despite the skip, those facts would be silently excluded from the next dedup window. No test exercises this path end-to-end via `engine.consolidate()`. The sentinel contract is documented only in a comment.

## Suggested approach
Add an integration test that: (1) inserts at least two near-duplicate facts, (2) directly manipulates the store to make `list_active` return a list longer than `MAX_DEDUP_FACTS` (e.g., by temporarily lowering the cap via a feature flag or by inserting inline via `FactStore`), (3) calls `consolidate()`, and (4) asserts `get_config("last_consolidated_at")` is still `None` (or unchanged from before). Because 50_000 is too large to insert in a test, a better approach is to expose the cap as a testable constant or add a `#[cfg(test)]` override path.

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**greedy_cluster() has algebraic invariants well-suited for property-based testing**

- **ID:** `consolidation/testing-proptest-greedy-cluster-invariants`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** consolidation · **Type:** test
- **Location:** `src/consolidation/cluster.rs:106-140`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`proptest` is already a dev-dependency (Cargo.toml:41) and is used in `src/search/hybrid.rs` and `src/search/vector.rs`. `greedy_cluster()` has strong structural invariants that example-based tests cannot adequately cover: (1) **partition**: every index 0..n appears in exactly one cluster; (2) **within-cluster similarity**: for any two facts in the same cluster, there exists a chain of pairwise-similar facts connecting them; (3) **between-cluster dissimilarity**: no fact in cluster A is similar (> threshold) to a fact in cluster B; (4) **monotonicity**: lowering the threshold never reduces cluster count. None of these are verified.

## Suggested approach
Add a `#[cfg(test)] mod proptest_greedy_cluster` block in cluster.rs (mirroring `proptest_rrf` in hybrid.rs). Generate random `Vec<Fact>` with random unit-normalized embeddings and random thresholds in [0.0, 1.0]. Assert partition invariant: `clusters.iter().flatten().sorted().collect::<Vec<_>>() == (0..n).collect::<Vec<_>>()`. Assert no index appears twice. The similarity-chain and monotonicity properties can be checked with bounded exhaustive loops over the generated data.

**No fuzz targets exist; multiple deserialization entry-points are unfuzzed**

- **Area:** core · **Type:** test
- **Location:** `src/types.rs, src/async_engine.rs`

## Description
The `fuzz/` directory is absent. The following types in scope are derived `Deserialize` and serve as entry-points for untrusted bytes: `Event`, `Fact`, `Edge`, `Summary`, `NewEvent`, `NewFact`, `PromotionProvenance`, `LineageRecord`, `LineageSnapshotEntry`, `Activity`, `SessionCheckpoint`, `Insight`, `CycleReport`. The MCP server (separate crate, not in scope) deserializes JSON from network; its payloads eventually flow through these types. `MemoryError::Serialization` (`#[from] serde_json::Error` at error.rs:11) is the expected failure mode — but whether deserialization panics on structurally valid but semantically extreme inputs (e.g. 768-dim embedding JSON with `Infinity` floats, or `importance` outside [0,1]) is untested. `Cargo.toml` has no `cargo-fuzz` or `libfuzzer-sys` dependency.

## Suggested approach
Add a `fuzz/` directory with at least one target targeting `serde_json::from_str::<Fact>` over arbitrary bytes. Cargo-fuzz initialization:
```
cargo fuzz init
cargo fuzz add fuzz_fact_deserialize
```
Fuzz target body:
```rust
#![no_main]
use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target;
fuzz_target!(|data: &[u8]| {
    if let Ok(s) = std::str::from_utf8(data) {
        let _ = serde_json::from_str::<memory_engine::types::Fact>(s);
    }
});
```

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**`MockEmbedder` returns a constant vector, masking vector-ranking correctness**

- **ID:** `engine/mock-constant-embedder-masks-ranking`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** core · **Type:** test
- **Location:** `src/engine/tests.rs:~line 20-35 (MockEmbedder definition)`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`MockEmbedder` always returns `vec![0.5; dim]` for every input. All vector similarity tests therefore see identical cosine scores for all facts, effectively disabling the vector ranking component of hybrid search. Any bug in the HNSW / vector-distance path that produces wrong ordering between distinct embeddings would go undetected. The `ReverseReranker` compensates for reranker ordering tests, but the embedding path itself (ANN distances, RRF weight blending) is never tested with distinguishable vectors in the main `tests.rs` suite.

## Suggested approach
Add a `DeterministicEmbedder` to a shared `test_utils` module that maps known keywords to fixed orthogonal vectors (e.g., `"cats" → [1,0,0,0]`, `"dogs" → [0,1,0,0]`). Use it in at least two vector-search tests to verify that `query` returns the semantically closest fact first by cosine similarity. This makes the embedding path a real discriminant rather than a tie between constant vectors.

manifest.body:
> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**`cosine_similarity` silently truncates mismatched-length slices — behavior undocumented and untested**

- **ID:** `search/testing-cosine-mismatched-length`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** retrieval · **Type:** test
- **Location:** `src/search/vector.rs:19-28`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
`cosine_similarity` uses `a.iter().zip(b.iter())` at line 21, which silently computes similarity over the prefix of the shorter slice when `a.len() != b.len()`. This is a public `#[must_use]` function with no length check and no test for the mismatched case. No doc comment mentions truncation behavior. Callers computing partial inner products against higher-dimensional vectors will get a silently wrong result. The proptest strategies at line 284/305 enforce `len = a.len().min(b.len())` before calling, masking the issue. CWE-129 (unchecked slice indexing), CWE-682 (incorrect calculation).

## Suggested approach
Either:
(a) Add a runtime check: `assert_eq!(a.len(), b.len(), "cosine_similarity: length mismatch")` and a test for the panic;
or (b) Document the truncation behavior explicitly in the doc comment and add a test:
```rust
#[test]
fn cosine_mismatched_length_truncates_to_shorter() {
    let a = [1.0_f32, 0.0, 0.0];
    let b = [1.0_f32, 0.0]; // shorter
    let sim = cosine_similarity(&a, &b);
    // zip truncates: computes similarity of [1,0] vs [1,0] = 1.0
    assert!((sim - 1.0).abs() < f32::EPSILON);
}
```
Option (a) is safer for an internal-use function whose callers already check dimension uniformity at the store level.

## References
CWE-682, CWE-129

<!-- super-qa-key: search/testing-cosine-mismatched-length -->

> ⚠️ Generated by `/super-qa` 2026-06-01. Severity & details from agent analysis; **not independently source-verified**. Review before action.

**Consolidate and forget pipelines have no integration-level test**

- **ID:** `store/integration-consolidate-forget`
- **Severity:** medium
- **Area:** storage · **Type:** test
- **Location:** `tests/roundtrip_test.rs`
- **Auto-fixable:** no

## Description
The roundtrip integration test covers ingest and query but not consolidate or forget. These are the two highest-complexity pipeline operations and have no end-to-end test through MemoryEngine — only unit-level tests (if any) within the engine module. A regression in the forget decay curve or the consolidation dedup pass would not be caught at the integration level.

## Suggested approach
Add integration tests that call MemoryEngine::consolidate() and MemoryEngine::forget() with mock trait implementations and assert post-conditions: facts below importance threshold are expired, duplicate facts are merged into summaries, etc.
